title: Cisco Duo Policy Allow Tampered Devices
exclusions: Detects the configuration change only. It does not show which sign-ins later used the weakened policy; correlate with the Duo authentication log for that.
evidence: Saved alert results with the administrator, policy name, and changed-settings JSON, plus the change ticket recorded in the response.

controlTest.positiveScenario: In a test Duo account, edit a policy so it allows rooted or jailbroken phones to approve Duo authentications, then save. Within one input interval an event with `action=policy_update` and `allow_rooted_devices=true` in `description` appears in `index=duo`, and the search returns one row naming the policy and the administrator.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Edit the same policy to change only its name or an unrelated setting. The administrator event is indexed, but the search returns no rows.

dataSources: `index=duo sourcetype=cisco:duo:administrator` from the Cisco Security Cloud (7404) Duo input, Administrator log type, which polls the Duo Admin API endpoint `GET /admin/v1/logs/administrator`. One event per administrator action.
app: Cisco Security Cloud (`CiscoSecurityCloud`, [Splunkbase 7404](https://splunkbase.splunk.com/app/7404)), Cisco Duo input. Replaces the deprecated Duo Splunk Connector (Splunkbase 3504, end of life 31 May 2026).
spl:
index=duo sourcetype="cisco:duo:administrator" (action="policy_update" OR action="policy_create")
| spath input=description
| search allow_rooted_devices=true
| rename object as policy_name
| stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(description) as description by action actionlabel policy_name username admin_email
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
description: Finds Duo policy creations and updates in the administrator log whose settings JSON sets `allow_rooted_devices` to the value that allows rooted or jailbroken phones to approve Duo authentications. Returns the policy, the administrator, and the full changed-settings description.
value: Rooted and jailbroken phones can run malware that reads or auto-approves Duo Push. Allowing them removes the device-integrity guarantee the second factor depends on.
implementation: Collect the Duo Administrator log with the Cisco Security Cloud (7404) Duo input into `index=duo`. The search parses the `description` JSON with `spath` and matches `allow_rooted_devices=true`. Alert on every hit and require a change ticket for each one.
visualization: Alert table: firstTime, lastTime, username, admin_email, policy_name, action, description. Supporting panel: 90-day count of policy changes by administrator (bar chart).

references.title: Cisco Security Cloud App for Splunk User Guide

knownFalsePositives:
1. **Approved exception policies** — some groups (kiosks, service desks, lab tenants) legitimately need a policy that allows rooted or jailbroken phones to approve Duo authentications. Keep those policy names in a lookup and exclude them only after the exception is approved.

2. **Policy copies** — cloning an existing policy logs a `policy_create` with the inherited settings even though no administrator chose them. Check `actionlabel` and whether the source policy already had the setting.

**Suppression:** a lookup of approved policy names with an owner and expiry date, applied after `stats`.
detailedImplementation:
Prerequisites
• Cisco Security Cloud (`CiscoSecurityCloud`, Splunkbase 7404) on the search heads and on the heavy forwarder or Splunk Cloud Inputs Data Manager that runs its modular inputs. It replaces the Duo Splunk Connector (Splunkbase 3504, end of life 31 May 2026); disable the old connector's inputs after cutover so events are not indexed twice.
• A Duo Admin API application created by an Owner-role administrator in the Duo Admin Panel under Applications > Protect an Application > Admin API. Record the integration key, secret key, and API hostname (`api-XXXXXXXX.duosecurity.com`), and grant it **Grant read log**.
• Outbound HTTPS (TCP 443) from the input host to the API hostname, and an accurate system clock on that host, because the Admin API signs every request with the current date.
• An index for Duo data (this page uses `index=duo`) and a role with `srchIndexesAllowed` on it for the identity and SOC teams.

Step 1 — Configure data collection
• In Cisco Security Cloud open Application Setup, choose the Cisco Duo card, and create an input with the integration key, secret key, and API hostname. Enable the Administrator log type and set the index to `duo`.
• The input reads `GET /admin/v1/logs/administrator` and writes `sourcetype=cisco:duo:administrator`, one event per administrator action, with `action`, `actionlabel`, `description` (a JSON string of the changed settings), `object` (the policy, user, or integration acted on), and `username` (the administrator).
• Check the field this search needs: run `index=duo sourcetype=cisco:duo:administrator action=policy_update | spath input=description | stats count by allow_rooted_devices` over 30 days and confirm `allow_rooted_devices` is populated.

Step 2 — Create the search and alert
```spl
index=duo sourcetype="cisco:duo:administrator" (action="policy_update" OR action="policy_create")
| spath input=description
| search allow_rooted_devices=true
| rename object as policy_name
| stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(description) as description by action actionlabel policy_name username admin_email
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
```

Understanding this SPL
• The first line limits the search to policy creations and updates in the Duo administrator log.
• `spath input=description` turns the JSON string of changed settings into fields; `allow_rooted_devices=true` is the value that allows rooted or jailbroken phones to approve Duo authentications.
• `object` holds the policy name in policy events, so it is renamed `policy_name`; `username` and `admin_email` identify who made the change.
• `stats ... values(description)` keeps the full changed-settings JSON on the row for the reviewer.

Step 3 — Validate
• Compare with the Duo admin console (Admin Panel) under Reports > Administrator Actions for the same time range: every policy change listed there should appear as an event in `index=duo`.
• Open the matching policy in the Admin Panel under Policies and confirm the setting shown matches the `description` JSON on the alert row.
• Run `index=duo sourcetype=cisco:duo:administrator | timechart span=1h count` over 7 days; gaps longer than two input intervals point to collection failures, not quiet periods.

Step 4 — Operationalize
• Schedule every 15 minutes over the last 20 minutes and throttle on `policy_name` plus `username` for 24 hours, so one change produces one alert.
• Route to the identity team with the Duo change ticket number as a required field in the response, and send to Enterprise Security as a finding when ES is in use.
• Keep a 90-day table panel of all policy changes next to this alert, so reviewers can see what else the same administrator changed.

Step 5 — Troubleshooting
• No Duo events and HTTP 401 in the input log under `$SPLUNK_HOME/var/log/splunk/duo_splunkapp/`: wrong secret key, an API hostname from a different Duo account, or clock skew on the input host.
• HTTP 403: the Admin API application is missing **Grant read log**.
• HTTP 429: Duo rate-limits the log endpoints. Make sure the deprecated 3504 connector and the 7404 input are not both polling the same Admin API application.
• Duplicate rows after migration: the 3504 connector and the 7404 input are both enabled for the same log type.
• Search runs but `allow_rooted_devices` is empty: the policy event's `description` uses a different key in your Duo release. Inspect one raw `policy_update` event and adjust the `search` line.
grandmaExplanation: We watch for anyone changing Duo so that hacked or jailbroken phones can approve logins.
